title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: GAR 4 — Decalogue metaphors; PLAC tip before Denique
pass_a_gloss: GAR. 4. That laws ought to be conceived in usual words, that is, commonly known, we confess. But who would say metaphorical and improper words are not usual? Indeed nothing is more common than metaphors, even in enacting laws, which often embrace many things in one voice, and those most diverse, so that they cannot be reduced to the propriety of one vocabulary-item, as is plain in the precepts of the Decalogue. PLAC. Did I say metaphorical and improper words are not usual? I said only that the name of death in that metaphorical and improper sense in which it signifies spiritual death, or the privation of original righteousness, is not usual in the Old Testament. I did not deny that metaphors are sometimes used in laws; I only denied that those are used which at the time when laws are made are unusual: I also denied that the same voice once used in the same law ought to be understood at once both properly and metaphorically. For then at last it ought to be taken metaphorically when something stands in the way so that it cannot or ought not to be taken properly. Nor do I on that account deny a double sense of Scripture, literal and mystical: for that is of the words, this rather of the things. In the precepts of the Decalogue I see no voice which ought to be expounded at once both properly and improperly, or metaphorically.
pass_b_english: GAR. 4. We grant that laws should be framed in ordinary, commonly known words. But who says metaphorical or improper words are not ordinary? Metaphors are nowhere more common than in framing laws, which often pack many and very different things into one word that cannot be reduced to a single proper sense—as the Decalogue's precepts show.

PLAC. Did I say metaphorical and improper words are unused? I said only that 'death' in the metaphorical, improper sense that means spiritual death—or the privation of original righteousness—is unused in the Old Testament. I never denied that laws sometimes use metaphors; I denied using metaphors that were unusual when the laws were made, and I denied that the same word, used once in the same law, must be read both properly and metaphorically at once. Metaphor comes in only when something blocks taking the word properly. That does not make me deny Scripture's double sense, literal and mystical: the first belongs to the words, the second rather to the things. In the Decalogue I see no word that must be read both properly and improperly—or metaphorically—together.
source_text: GAR. 4. Verbis usitatis, id est, vulgo notis leges concipi debere fatemur. Sed quis dicat verba metaphorica & impropria non esse usitata? Imo metaphoris nihil communius, etiam in legibus sanciendis, quae saepe una voce multa complectuntur, eaque diversissima, ut ad unius vocabuli proprietatem redigi non possint, sicuti patet in praeceptis Decalogi. PLAC. Dixine verba metaphorica, & impropria non esse usitata? Dixi tantum nomen mortis eo sensu metaphorico & improprio, quo significat mortem spiritualem, seu privationem justitiae originalis, non esse usitatum in vetere Testamento. Non negavi quin usurpentur interdum metaphorae in legibus, tantum negavi eas usurpari, quae sunt eo tempore, quo leges feruntur, inusitatae: negavi etiam eandem vocem in eadem lege semel usurpatam, simul & proprie & metaphorice intelligi debere. Tum enim demum accipi debet metaphorice, cum aliquid obest, quominus accipi possit aut debeat proprie. Neque propterea duplicem sensum Scripturae nego, literalem & mysticum: ille enim est verborum, hic potius rerum. In praeceptis Decalogi nullam vocem video, quae simul & proprie & improprie, seu metaphorice debeat exponi.

choices.choice: Decalogue metaphors != same word proper+metaphorical at once
